newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Short day, but bears still rule.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Short day, but bears still rule.

text.p: The negative sentiment that has prevailed in the U.S. Treasury market is expected to continue Friday, although any further damage is seen limited as the market closes early ahead of the long holiday weekend.
PSA The Bond Market Trade Association has recommended a 1400 EST/1900 GMT close in observance of the Martin Luther King Jr holiday, which will keep the market closed on Monday.
"In front of the three-day weekend, we may be active until 1000 (EST) and that's it," said one head trader at a large U.S. bank.
But despite the pre-holiday environment, the market has a lot to digest by 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

At 0830 EST/1330 GMT, the Commerce Department will release November international trade figures, followed at 0915 EST/1414 GMT by the Federal Reserve's industrial production/capacity utilization report for December. At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the University of Michigan is expected to release its preliminary January consumer sentiment index.

According to Reuters polls, the trade deficit is seen widening to $9.8 billion in November from $7.99 billion in October; production is expected to have jumped 0.6 percent in December, with the capacity utilization rate up 0.2 point to 83.5 percent and the Michigan index is seen up 1.4 points to 98.3.
Numbers at or above consensus are seen bearish, players said.
"For the Treasury market, the U.S. economy is firming and (recent strong economic) numbers are not an abberation," said a trader at a primary dealership.

Traders said the data released in recent weeks should have sent Treasuries down much further, but resurgent European and Japanese bond markets, along with a continued strong dollar, prevented heavier losses. The dollar is seen coming under more scrutiny on Friday to see how it reacts to the trade figures, particularly imports and exports with Japan.

Meanwhile, the large corporate bond issuance continues to rattle Treasuries, particularly the record issue by US West. Thursday. US West upped its five-part bond offer to $4.1 billion from $3.5 billion on Wednesday.

Traders said hedging on Treasuries contributed heavily to the 30-year bond's half-point fall on Thursday. Bearish comments from Federal Reserve governor Laurence Meyer, who suggested wage inflation is becoming a problem, also hurt the market. Players expected Treasury yields to continue rising, with the long bond breaching seven percent and the two-year note jumping above 6.25 percent in the near future.
Supply continues to be a dominant force and should be for some time, traders said, as the market faces more than $100 billion in upcoming Treasury supply the next five weeks.
Still, no new ranges are expected to be made until at least January 28, the day the fourth-quarter employment cost index will be released, players said.
